content.title: AEW Revolution 2026 results, grades, awards: MJF beats Hangman Page in gruesome instant classic
content.text: AEW Revolution 2026 lived up to its name once again. The stacked lineup of professional wrestling action touched down at Los Angeles' Crypto.com Arena, leaving the community's collective breath taken away.Last year's spring spectacular was great, just as most AEW pay-per-views usually are. However, Sunday's latest installment entirely surpassed Revolution 2025 and even leaned more toward Double or Nothing 2025's all-timer status, if you ask yours truly.AdvertisementTruly, where do we even begin?Obviously it has to be the night’s unimaginably gruesome main event, which centered around the AEW World Championship and changed the entire landscape of the title picture. The world champion MJF successfully defended against "Hangman" Adam Page, costing Page any future title opportunities after "Hangman" came short for the first time in his AEW career in his patented Texas Deathmatch.This match was pure wrestling cinema, just like Page's last match of this ilk was when he dethroned Jon Moxley at All In 2025. But when I say "cinema," please understand that we're talking about a horror flick rollercoaster ride. MJF and Page's world championship blood feud went anywhere and everywhere. From syringe impalement to deep-pocket dog-collar storytelling, there was almost too much packed into this match. I'll repeat this any time it's necessary: It's unreal how creative AEW continues to manage to be with matches of this caliber — spot and storytelling-wise.Although there were several opportunities to give the match a perfect ending, the finishing sequence somehow superseded all prior false-endings. Unlike his victory over Moxley, the chain and dog collar became Page's demise in the most impactful loss of his career. The more I soak in the match, the more it triggers a desire to break my five-star scale. Nonetheless, this was masterful work from AEW's greatest hero and greatest villain. Once again, these two have reshaped the company's future in the most compelling way un-imaginable — because somehow, AEW continues to break my perceived boundaries of wrestling creativity.It should come as no surprise that an AEW pay-per-view closed with a perfect five-star match, but when it starts with one, you know you're in for a treat. That's what we got with another instant classic, as FTR successfully defended their AEW Tag Team Championships against the Young Bucks. Go ahead and buy the pay-per-view replay right this second, then watch it after you finish reading here. It's entirely worth it and then some.AdvertisementThe aftermath of the match set the tone for one of two big returns, as Adam Copeland and Christian Cage returned with revenge on their minds against FTR. There was a Bucks tease too, which leads me to the thought of AEW's own TLC chaos in the near future. Yes, Cope & Cage are a bit too old for the stipulation they founded, but how wild would that be? Nonetheless, FTR vs. Cope & Cage is the clear next direction, and rightfully so.Will Ospreay highlighted the other return of the night, following AEW Revolution's other five-star banger between Jon Moxley and Konosuke Takeshita. Looking beefier than ever before, but just as nimble as we remember him, Ospreay took out Moxley and the Death Riders after Moxley's phenomenal defense of the AEW Continental Championship.AdvertisementBut the largest surprise of the night easily came when former UFC and WWE champion Ronda Rousey entered the AEW ring after Toni Storm's win over Marina Shafir. Rousey and Shafir have a longtime friendship, going back to their days as teammates in MMA — which Rousey will return to against Gina Carano in May. Until then, it appears there are wheels in motion for a potential program between Rousey and Storm, the latter of whom put on her typical entertaining match against Shafir.As for the woman holding Storm's former strap, Thekla closed out her AEW Women's Championship feud with Kris Statlander, beating her 2-to-1 in their Two-Out-Of-Three-Falls Match. The expected interferences from the Sisters of Sin soured the finish of the match a bit, but overall there's been great chemistry and history now built between the rivals. AEW has plenty to work with here down the road.Elsewhere on the card, three titles changed hands. First, Ricochet came up short in the Zero Hour pre-show 21-Man Blackjack Battle Royal for his AEW National Championship, as Jack Perry got the last laugh and claimed the title. The same could be said for the Divine Dominion (Megan Bayne and Lena Kross), who dethroned the AEW Women's Tag Team Champions, the Babes of Wrath (Harley Cameron and Willow Nightingale). Lastly, JetSpeed (Kevin Knight and Mike Bailey), alongside the newly signed Mistico, dethroned the Don Callis Family to become the new AEW Trios Champions.AdvertisementAEW pay-per-views are always a pretty lengthy events. But when they're of such high quality, that length is barely noticed or even really an issue. This was one of those nights you hoped would never end. No (more) notes, Tony Khan. Keep it up.AEW Revolution 2026 crown score: 👑 10/10 👑AEW Revolution 2026 Uncrowned AwardsMVP(s) of the Night: MJF and Hangman Adam PageCould it be any other duo? The lengths MJF and Page were willing to go to for their craft are, quite frankly, sickening. As mentioned, they packed absolutely everything into their match and didn't undersell a single moment. It legitimately felt as if we were witnessing several murder attempts, which was the embodiment of a Texas Deathmatch's point. Plus, of course, the fact that Page's championship aspirations were on the line. They made you believe. And you can't ask for anything more than that.AdvertisementUncrowned Gem of the Night: Jon Moxley vs. Konosuke TakeshitaA usual suspect and contender for MVP, Moxley took a backseat tonight. It was the Takeshita show, as this guy once again displayed how much of a made man and legend in the making that he is. He isn't aura farming, he's aura creating. The duo paired phenomenally once again, delivering their best match yet without time restrictions, and Takeshita proved he needed to be killed to be stopped. It was a version of the main event match — without the heavy layers of violence. A masterclass.Match of the Night: FTR vs. The Young BucksAnd somehow, despite all that was just said, neither of those two matches were the best of the night. The Young Bucks and FTR very well could be the two greatest tag-teams of all time. Take your pick, I don't care. It's the Bucks in my books. No matter what, they don't miss, and when tag-team wrestling is at its best, there is absolutely nothing like it. This match was visual eyeball glue, forcing you to keeping watching because it was so damn entertaining throughout.AdvertisementI don't want to compare, but I have to: When you see matches like this, you can't help but feel insanely embarrassed by how WWE treats tag-team wrestling.Best Spot(s) of the Night: Clark Connors' spear to Darby Allin through the ropes and Hangman Adam Page's Buckshot Lariat to MJF with skewers in his headThis is the one award that always has ties, isn't it?Realistically, I could have split this about five different ways. For starters, Clark Connors speared the ever-loving daylights out of Darby Allin with what may have been the greatest — and gnarliest — apron spear of all time.But remember those perfect-finish opportunities I mentioned in MJF vs. Page? Well, the first one came at the expense of MJF, who had skewers jammed into his wonderful new hairline. The jockey for position was wonderful violence-drama to start, but then Page made contact.AdvertisementIt felt like that was the spot, and they were moving on.Nope.Page went to the apron for the Buckshot Lariat, and the skewers bursted out of MJF's head on contact, creating a visual that would put tonight's Oscar winners to shame. It's too poetic that those two events coincided, really. If Page had been booked to win, this would've been the moment. Beautiful.AEW Revolution 2026 full card results, grades and highlights:AEW World Championship - Last Chance Texas Deathmatch: MJF (c.) def.
